title: Sacubitril/Valsartan: ARNI Safety, Washout, and Potassium
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Sacubitril/valsartan combines neprilysin inhibition with angiotensin-receptor blockade for selected heart-failure patients. Safe use requires attention to blood pressure, renal function, potassium, angioedema risk, pregnancy, and the required separation from ACE inhibitors.
recognize: Hypotension, rising creatinine, hyperkalemia, or facial/tongue swelling may signal clinically important toxicity.
Concurrent ACE-inhibitor exposure creates unacceptable angioedema risk and requires a washout interval before ARNI use.
priorities: Verify the medication history for ACE inhibitors, ARBs, aliskiren, potassium supplements, and potassium-sparing drugs.
Assess BP, renal function, potassium, pregnancy status when relevant, and any history of angioedema.
Escalate airway swelling, severe hypotension, major hyperkalemia, or acute renal deterioration.
assessMonitor: Trend BP, dizziness/orthostasis, creatinine/eGFR, potassium, volume status, and heart-failure symptoms.
interventions: Administer consistently as ordered and reinforce daily weight/symptom monitoring in heart failure.
medicationSafety: Do not overlap with an ACE inhibitor; current labeling requires separation because of angioedema risk.
The current U.S. label carries a boxed warning for fetal toxicity.
teaching: Do not restart an old ACE inhibitor or potassium supplement without clinician review; report swelling or fainting immediately.
delegationScope: Routine administration/monitoring may be within PN scope; initiation, titration, and management of unstable heart failure require RN/provider collaboration.
examTrap: Giving sacubitril/valsartan immediately after the last ACE-inhibitor dose because both treat heart failure.
oneLinePearl: ARNI safety = no ACE overlap, watch pressure, kidneys, potassium, and swelling.

title: Ivabradine: Slow the Sinus Node Without Dropping Contractility
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Ivabradine lowers heart rate by inhibiting the sinoatrial If current and is used in selected patients with heart failure who remain in sinus rhythm. The major safety issues are bradycardia, conduction problems, atrial fibrillation, and transient visual brightness phenomena.
recognize: The drug works through the sinus node, so rhythm matters; it is not a generic rate-control substitute for atrial fibrillation.
New irregular pulse, symptomatic bradycardia, or dizziness warrants evaluation.
priorities: Verify sinus rhythm, resting pulse, BP, and interacting rate-slowing medications.
Escalate syncope, marked bradycardia, new atrial fibrillation, or heart-failure deterioration.
assessMonitor: Trend heart rate/rhythm, BP, dizziness, fatigue, visual symptoms, and heart-failure status.
interventions: Administer on schedule and monitor response rather than chasing one isolated pulse reading.
medicationSafety: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors can substantially increase exposure.
Concurrent negative chronotropes can increase bradycardia risk.
teaching: Report fainting, a new irregular heartbeat, or severe dizziness; brief luminous visual phenomena can occur but still should be discussed if troublesome.
delegationScope: Routine pulse checks may be delegated with clear thresholds; interpretation of new rhythm change requires licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Using ivabradine as if it treats any tachyarrhythmia regardless of rhythm.
oneLinePearl: Ivabradine slows sinus rate—so first confirm the rhythm is sinus.

title: Ranolazine: Chronic Angina Without Acute Rescue
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Ranolazine is used for chronic angina symptom control; it is not a rescue drug for an acute coronary syndrome. Safety centers on QT prolongation, CYP3A interactions, renal/hepatic context, dizziness, and medication reconciliation.
recognize: New palpitations, syncope, or marked QT prolongation is more concerning than common dizziness or constipation.
Strong CYP3A inhibitors can markedly raise ranolazine exposure.
priorities: Review ECG/QT risk, kidney/liver disease, and the complete medication list for CYP3A or QT-prolonging interactions.
Escalate acute chest pain as possible ischemia rather than giving extra ranolazine as rescue.
assessMonitor: Trend angina frequency, dizziness, BP, ECG/QT when indicated, renal function, and interacting drugs.
interventions: Continue prescribed antianginal plan and ensure acute-chest-pain instructions are separately understood.
medicationSafety: Do not use as immediate relief for acute chest pain.
Avoid unsafe CYP3A combinations and cumulative QT risk.
complications: Persistent ischemia if acute symptoms are mismanaged
teaching: Keep the separate emergency chest-pain plan; ranolazine is maintenance therapy, not a fast-acting nitrate.
delegationScope: Medication administration and routine symptom collection may be within PN scope; acute chest-pain evaluation requires immediate escalation.
examTrap: Telling a patient to take extra ranolazine for sudden crushing chest pain.
oneLinePearl: Ranolazine prevents angina symptoms; it does not rescue acute ischemia.

title: Sotalol: Beta Blocker Plus QT Risk
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Sotalol combines beta-blockade with class III antiarrhythmic effects. It can slow heart rate and prolong QT, so renal function, electrolytes, ECG/QT, and interacting QT-prolonging drugs are central to safe therapy.
recognize: Bradycardia, prolonged QT, low potassium/magnesium, and renal impairment increase torsades risk.
New syncope or polymorphic ventricular rhythm is an emergency.
priorities: Verify renal function, potassium/magnesium, heart rate, ECG/QT, and concurrent QT-prolonging drugs.
Escalate syncope, severe bradycardia, marked QT prolongation, or ventricular dysrhythmia.
assessMonitor: Trend ECG/QT, pulse, BP, potassium, magnesium, renal function, and symptoms.
interventions: Follow the ordered initiation/reinitiation monitoring pathway and do not independently alter the schedule.
medicationSafety: Renal clearance makes kidney function clinically important.
Avoid stacking QT-prolonging medications or ignoring electrolyte depletion.
teaching: Do not double missed doses; report fainting or new palpitations immediately.
delegationScope: Antiarrhythmic initiation/monitoring requires facility-defined competency; new rhythm abnormalities require licensed-nurse escalation.
examTrap: Focusing only on beta-blocker effects and forgetting sotalol can prolong QT and cause torsades.
oneLinePearl: Sotalol slows the pulse and lengthens repolarization—watch rate, QT, kidneys, K, and Mg.

title: Flecainide: Class IC Rhythm Control and Proarrhythmia
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Flecainide is a class IC antiarrhythmic used in carefully selected patients. It can widen conduction intervals and provoke dangerous arrhythmias, especially in structural heart disease or ischemic scar, so rhythm, conduction, renal/hepatic context, and symptoms must be monitored closely.
recognize: New wide-complex tachycardia, syncope, worsening heart failure, or major QRS/PR changes can indicate proarrhythmia or toxicity.
It is not a benign general-purpose rhythm drug for every patient with palpitations.
priorities: Confirm the indication and review structural/ischemic heart disease, ECG, renal/hepatic function, and interacting AV-node drugs.
Escalate syncope, ventricular dysrhythmia, new conduction block, or heart-failure worsening.
assessMonitor: Trend ECG/rhythm, QRS/PR changes, pulse, BP, renal/hepatic status, dizziness, and dyspnea.
interventions: Administer exactly as prescribed and maintain planned ECG follow-up.
medicationSafety: Class IC agents can be proarrhythmic in patients with structural ischemic heart disease.
Conduction slowing can become clinically important when combined with other rate/conduction-slowing drugs.
teaching: Report fainting, worsening shortness of breath, or a new sustained rapid heartbeat promptly.
delegationScope: Routine administration may be within PN scope; antiarrhythmic initiation, ECG interpretation, and instability require RN/provider collaboration.
examTrap: Assuming flecainide is safe for rhythm control in any patient with prior myocardial infarction.
oneLinePearl: Flecainide can organize rhythm or provoke it—structural heart disease and ECG changes matter.

title: Isosorbide Mononitrate: Prevent Angina, Do Not Chase Acute Pain
bottomLine: Isosorbide mononitrate is a long-acting nitrate used to prevent angina. It is not intended for immediate relief of an acute attack; hypotension, headache, nitrate tolerance, and dangerous phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor interactions are the main safety issues.
recognize: Headache and dizziness are common vasodilator effects; syncope or profound hypotension is not routine.
PDE-5 inhibitors and soluble-guanylate-cyclase stimulators can produce dangerous hypotension with nitrates.
priorities: Check BP, orthostatic symptoms, medication list, and acute-chest-pain plan.
Escalate acute ischemic symptoms rather than substituting maintenance nitrate for emergency evaluation.
assessMonitor: Trend angina frequency, BP, dizziness, headache burden, and adherence to the prescribed nitrate-free strategy if applicable.
interventions: Administer on the prescribed schedule and reinforce separate short-acting rescue/emergency instructions.
medicationSafety: Do not combine with PDE-5 inhibitors or riociguat-type therapy.
Do not crush extended-release formulations unless product instructions allow it.
teaching: This medicine prevents attacks; it is not the drug to rely on when sudden ischemic chest pain begins.
delegationScope: Administration and routine BP monitoring may be within PN scope; acute chest pain requires immediate licensed assessment/escalation.
examTrap: Using long-acting isosorbide mononitrate as the first rescue treatment for acute chest pain.
oneLinePearl: Long-acting nitrate prevents; it does not rescue.

title: Ezetimibe: Cholesterol Absorption Blocker and Combination Safety
bottomLine: Ezetimibe lowers LDL cholesterol by reducing intestinal cholesterol absorption and is often used with statin therapy when additional LDL reduction is needed. Nursing safety centers on adherence, liver/muscle symptoms in combination therapy, and recognizing that lipid lowering is preventive rather than symptom-relieving.
recognize: Patients may feel no different even when therapy is working.
Unexplained muscle pain or jaundice warrants review, especially when combined with a statin.
priorities: Review the complete lipid-lowering regimen, liver disease, muscle symptoms, and adherence.
Escalate severe muscle weakness, dark urine, or hepatic-injury symptoms.
assessMonitor: Trend lipid results, adherence, liver-related symptoms/labs when ordered, and muscle complaints.
interventions: Reinforce diet/activity and secondary-prevention measures alongside medication therapy.
medicationSafety: Combination with statins can increase the relevance of liver and muscle monitoring.
Bile-acid sequestrants can affect absorption timing.
teaching: Continue therapy even when you feel well; LDL lowering prevents events rather than treating immediate symptoms.
delegationScope: Routine administration and adherence reinforcement may be within PN scope; treatment escalation is prescriber-directed.
examTrap: Stopping ezetimibe because the patient reports no symptomatic improvement despite a lower LDL level.
oneLinePearl: Ezetimibe is prevention medicine—judge it by LDL and risk, not by how the patient feels today.

title: Evolocumab: PCSK9 Inhibition and Injection Safety
bottomLine: Evolocumab is a PCSK9 inhibitor that markedly lowers LDL cholesterol in selected patients. Safe use depends on correct subcutaneous device technique, adherence to the dosing schedule, monitoring lipid response, and recognizing hypersensitivity or injection-site problems.
recognize: Local injection reactions and upper-respiratory symptoms can occur; generalized swelling or breathing difficulty suggests hypersensitivity.
The drug does not replace acute ACS treatment or lifestyle/other secondary-prevention measures.
priorities: Verify the prescribed device/schedule and teach storage, warming-to-room-temperature instructions, site rotation, and device completion according to product directions.
Escalate systemic hypersensitivity.
assessMonitor: Trend LDL response, adherence, injection-site reactions, and allergy symptoms.
interventions: Use teach-back with the actual injection device when self-administration is planned.
medicationSafety: Do not confuse the available device presentations or dosing schedules.
Inspect product and follow current storage instructions before injection.
complications: Loss of LDL control from missed doses
teaching: Keep scheduled doses and continue the broader cardiovascular-risk-reduction plan.
delegationScope: Subcutaneous administration and reinforcement may be within PN scope; lipid-treatment selection remains prescriber-directed.
examTrap: Assuming an injectable lipid drug is used for immediate treatment during an acute coronary syndrome.
oneLinePearl: PCSK9 therapy lowers long-term LDL risk—device technique and adherence make it work.

title: Clonidine: Central Alpha-2 Effects and Rebound Hypertension
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Clonidine reduces sympathetic outflow and can lower BP and heart rate, but abrupt discontinuation can cause marked rebound hypertension and adrenergic symptoms. Sedation, bradycardia, orthostasis, CNS-depressant interactions, and patch/tablet reconciliation are major nursing concerns.
recognize: Abrupt missed or stopped therapy can cause headache, agitation, tachycardia, and severe BP elevation.
Sedation and orthostasis can increase fall risk.
priorities: Verify formulation, schedule, BP, pulse, adherence, and sedating co-medications.
Escalate severe rebound hypertension, neurologic symptoms, chest pain, syncope, or marked bradycardia.
assessMonitor: Trend BP, pulse, orthostasis, sedation, adherence, and patch-site/patch-removal status when transdermal therapy is used.
interventions: Follow prescribed tapering rather than abrupt cessation when therapy is being discontinued.
medicationSafety: Do not stop clonidine suddenly unless directed in an emergency plan.
Medication reconciliation should prevent duplicate oral and transdermal exposure.
teaching: Never stop clonidine abruptly on your own; if a patch falls off or doses are missed, contact the care team for instructions.
delegationScope: Routine administration/vitals may be within PN scope; severe BP change or bradycardia requires licensed-nurse escalation.
examTrap: Holding several clonidine doses for mild drowsiness without a plan, then ignoring severe rebound hypertension.
oneLinePearl: Clonidine withdrawal can be more dangerous than clonidine drowsiness—never stop it casually.

title: Oral Hydralazine: Vasodilation, Reflex Tachycardia, and Lupus-Like Toxicity
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Oral hydralazine is a direct arterial vasodilator used in selected hypertension or heart-failure regimens. Safety centers on hypotension, reflex tachycardia, headache, fluid retention, and a lupus-like syndrome with longer exposure—not the rapid obstetric IV protocol taught elsewhere.
recognize: Dizziness, headache, tachycardia, or edema can reflect vasodilation/reflex physiology.
Arthralgia, fever, rash, pleuritic symptoms, or unexplained constitutional symptoms may suggest drug-induced lupus.
priorities: Check BP, pulse, edema/weight trend, adherence, and new inflammatory symptoms.
Escalate severe hypotension, ischemic chest pain, marked tachycardia, or suspected lupus-like toxicity.
assessMonitor: Trend BP, pulse, weight/edema, symptoms, and ordered CBC/autoimmune or renal studies if toxicity is suspected.
interventions: Administer on schedule and reinforce that abrupt self-adjustment can destabilize BP control.
medicationSafety: Reflex tachycardia and fluid retention may require companion therapy prescribed by the clinician.
This chronic oral lesson is not interchangeable with emergency IV hydralazine use in severe pregnancy hypertension.
teaching: Report persistent joint pain, fever, rash, chest pain, or worsening swelling rather than assuming they are expected effects.
delegationScope: Routine oral administration and vital monitoring may be within PN scope; unstable BP/cardiac symptoms require escalation.
examTrap: Treating chronic oral hydralazine monitoring as the same protocol as IV hydralazine for an obstetric emergency.
oneLinePearl: Hydralazine opens arteries—watch pressure, pulse, fluid, and lupus-like symptoms.
sourceBasis: DailyMed hydralazine hydrochloride oral labeling current 2026
